[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Disk Management in Linux (fdisk, parted, LVM)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"This tutorial covers disk management in Linux, focusing on partitioning tools (fdisk and parted) and Logical Volume Management (LVM). Understanding these tools is crucial for efficient storage utilization and system administration."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Partitioning with fdisk"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"fdisk is a command-line utility for partitioning disks. It's commonly used for MBR (Master Boot Record) disks. Note that fdisk has limitations with disks larger than 2TB."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"# fdisk /dev/sda"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command opens fdisk for the disk /dev/sda. Inside fdisk, you can use various commands:"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"m: Print the menu"},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"n: Add a new partition"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"d: Delete a partition"},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"p: Print the partition table"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"w: Write table to disk and exit"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"q: Quit without saving changes"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Example: To create a new primary partition, type 'n', then 'p', select the partition number (usually 1), and specify the first and last sectors. Accept the defaults to use the entire available space. Finally, type 'w' to write the changes."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Partitioning with parted"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"parted is a more advanced partitioning tool that supports GPT (GUID Partition Table) disks, which are necessary for disks larger than 2TB. It also offers more features than fdisk."},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"# parted /dev/sdb"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command opens parted for the disk /dev/sdb. Inside parted, you can use commands like:"},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"mklabel gpt: Create a GPT partition table"},{"order":19,"type":"bullet_point","text":"mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%: Create a primary partition using the entire disk formatted with ext4"},{"order":20,"type":"bullet_point","text":"print: Print the partition table"},{"order":21,"type":"bullet_point","text":"quit: Exit parted"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Example: To create a GPT partition table and a single ext4 partition, use the commands 'mklabel gpt' and 'mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%'. Then, type 'quit' to save the changes."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"Logical Volume Management (LVM)"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"LVM provides a flexible way to manage storage. It allows you to create logical volumes that can span multiple physical disks, be resized dynamically, and be easily snapshotted. LVM consists of Physical Volumes (PVs), Volume Groups (VGs), and Logical Volumes (LVs)."},{"order":25,"type":"paragraph","text":"1. Physical Volumes (PVs): These are the physical disks or partitions that LVM uses."},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"2. Volume Groups (VGs): A VG is a container for one or more PVs. It represents a pool of storage from which LVs can be created."},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"3. Logical Volumes (LVs): These are the virtual partitions that you can format and mount. They are created from the available space in a VG."},{"order":28,"type":"code","text":"# pvcreate /dev/sdc1
# vgcreate myvg /dev/sdc1
# lvcreate -L 10G -n mylv myvg"},{"order":29,"type":"paragraph","text":"These commands create a PV on /dev/sdc1, create a VG named 'myvg' using the PV, and then create an LV named 'mylv' with a size of 10GB from the VG."},{"order":30,"type":"code","text":"# mkfs.ext4 /dev/myvg/mylv
# mount /dev/myvg/mylv /mnt"},{"order":31,"type":"paragraph","text":"These commands format the LV with ext4 and mount it to /mnt."},{"order":32,"type":"subheading","text":"LVM Snapshots"},{"order":33,"type":"paragraph","text":"LVM snapshots allow you to create a point-in-time copy of an LV. This is useful for backups or testing changes without affecting the original data."},{"order":34,"type":"code","text":"# lvcreate -L 1G -s -n mylv_snap -p r /dev/myvg/mylv"},{"order":35,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command creates a snapshot named 'mylv_snap' of the LV 'mylv'. The '-s' option specifies that it's a snapshot, and '-p r' sets the snapshot to read-only."},{"order":36,"type":"subheading","text":"Resizing LVM Volumes"},{"order":37,"type":"paragraph","text":"LVM allows you to resize LVs dynamically without unmounting them."},{"order":38,"type":"code","text":"# lvextend -L +5G /dev/myvg/mylv
# resize2fs /dev/myvg/mylv"},{"order":39,"type":"paragraph","text":"These commands extend the LV 'mylv' by 5GB and then resize the filesystem to use the new space."},{"order":40,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":41,"type":"paragraph","text":"This tutorial provided an overview of disk management in Linux using fdisk, parted, and LVM. Mastering these tools is essential for managing storage effectively and ensuring the stability and performance of your Linux systems. Remember to always back up your data before making any changes to your disk configuration."}]
